extraction.name: CommonsenseQA
extraction.description: A challenging dataset for commonsense question answering containing 12,247 multiple-choice questions that require prior knowledge and common sense to answer. Questions are generated from ConceptNet by extracting source concepts and multiple target concepts with the same semantic relation, then asking crowd-workers to author questions that discriminate between the target concepts.
extraction.creator: Alon Talmor, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, Jonathan Berant
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions are generated through a multi-step crowdsourcing process using Amazon Mechanical Turk. Workers are shown a question concept and three answer concepts extracted from ConceptNet that share the same semantic relation. Workers formulate three questions (one per answer concept) where each question contains the question concept and has only one correct answer among the three concepts. Workers then add two additional distractors per question: one selected from ConceptNet and one manually authored.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: ConceptNet knowledge base containing 32 million triplets representing commonsense relations between natural language concepts. Triplets were filtered to 236,208 based on relation type, concept length, language, and edit distance criteria.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: ConceptNet triplets were filtered in three steps: (1) filtering triplets with general relations or relations well-explored in NLP, retaining 22 relations; (2) filtering triplets where concepts exceed four words or are not in English; (3) filtering triplets where edit distance between concepts is too low. Question sets were created by grouping three triplets with the same question concept and relation but different answer concepts. Questions were verified by workers and filtered if not verified by at least one worker, removing 15% of questions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Workers formulated three questions per question set, ensuring each question contains the question concept and has one correct answer among three semantically similar answer concepts. Workers were instructed to avoid using words strongly related to the answer concept to discourage simple surface clues. Workers added two distractors per question: one from ConceptNet and one manually authored to seem plausible but dismissible by humans. Only workers with at least 75% question pass rate in verification were accepted.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Each question was verified by 2 workers who either annotated it as unanswerable or chose the right answer. Questions were only retained if verified by at least one worker who answered correctly, filtering out 15% of questions. For human evaluation on a separate sample, majority vote was taken across five workers per question.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 verifiers per question during quality control; 5 workers per question for human evaluation sample
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: 122 formulators contributed to question generation, with 10 workers formulating more than 85% of the questions. Workers were required to have at least 75% of their questions pass verification. For human evaluation, workers were not AMT master workers and did not use a qualification test.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Analysis revealed that BERT-LARGE performs well (77.7% accuracy) on examples with surface clues hinting to the correct answer, suggesting potential bias toward surface-level patterns. The model shows lower accuracy on negation/antonym questions (42.8%), factoid knowledge questions (38.4%), questions requiring fine-grained distinctions (35.4%), and conjunction conditions (23.8%).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on commonsense knowledge encoded in ConceptNet and may not cover all types of commonsense reasoning. Questions are limited to 22 ConceptNet relations after filtering. The top-5 question concepts account for only 6.8% of questions, with 'Person' (3.1%), 'People' (2.0%), 'Human' (0.7%), 'Water' (0.5%) and 'Cat' (0.5%), suggesting concentration on certain concept types. Question formulators often created questions probing relationships beyond the original ConceptNet relation shown.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training and evaluating commonsense question answering systems. It can be used for testing models' ability to incorporate commonsense knowledge into NLU systems. The data was split into training/development/test sets with an 80/10/10 split, supporting both random split and question concept split evaluation modes.

name.evidence: To investigate question answering with prior knowledge, we present COMMONSENSE QA: a challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering.

description.evidence: To capture common sense beyond associations, we extract from CONCEPTNET (Speer et al., 2017) multiple target concepts that have the same semantic relation to a single source concept. Crowd-workers are asked to author multiple-choice questions that mention the source concept and discriminate in turn between each of the target concepts.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: We found that the model does well (77.7% accuracy) on examples where surface clues hint to the correct answer. Examples that involve negation or understanding antonyms have lower accuracy (42.8%), similarly to examples that require factoid knowledge (38.4%). Accuracy is particularly low in questions where the correct answer has finer granularity compared to one of the distractors (35.4%), and in cases where the correct answer needs to meet a conjunction of conditions, and the distractor meets only one of them (23.8%).
